title: 2025 Local Hiring Policy Annual Report published 04.01.25

sections.heading: Page 2
paragraphs: About OEWD and the Local Hiring Policy

sections.heading: Page 3
paragraphs: On behalf of the City of San Francisco, I am delighted to present the 2025 Annual Report on the Local Hiring Policy for Construction.
Though San Francisco has endured economic challenges in recent years, our workforce has been an integral part of rebuilding this
economy through one of our longest standing sectors, the construction trades. This sector has remained a strong and accessible career
path for many of San Francisco’s residents, supporting specialized training that results in jobs for our residents.
The Local Hiring Policy for Construction was designed to ensure local residents have access to meaningful career opportunities and
employment in the City. As commercial construction has slowed down, we are taking the initiative and continuing to invest in our City’s
infrastructure and housing stock. In 2025, San Francisco collected over 8 million hours of payroll submissions on construction-related
projects, of which 3.5 million hours were subject to local hiring requirements. These projects increase living spaces and improve public
safety. This report reflects that the Local Hiring Policy continues to provide opportunities for residents and communities across the City
As we look ahead at the exciting new developments on the horizon such as Potrero Power Station and Balboa Reservoir, we will lean in on
these tested and proven policies that create jobs and career paths for local workers. The Local Hiring Policy serves as a model for how
public-private partnerships in the construction industry create sustainable employment for residents. San Francisco's future is being
built today, with key projects that are contributing to its revitalization: UCSF's cutting-edge expansion at Parnassus Heights, the
transformation of Stonestown into a vibrant residential hub with 3,500 new homes, SF Gateway's 2 million square feet of PDR space for
industrial businesses, and the creation of an entirely new neighborhood on Treasure Island. To ensure our local workforce is ready to
capitalize on these opportunities, programs like CityBuild are providing critical skills training.
I am grateful for the many partners across the industry who help make the Local Hiring Policy a success. Thank you to the contractors,
industry employers, building and construction tr ades unions, community-base d organizations, and City departmen ts for their
contributions to bolstering our local construction sector. Your leadership is helping San Francisco come back stronger than ever, and
together we will continue to grow our economy, creating an environment where our local talent and companies can thrive. My
administration is excited to collaborate with our partners across the construction industry as we build the future of San Francisco.

paragraphs: The mission of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development
is to advance equitable and shared prosperity for San Franciscans
by growing sustainable jobs, supporting business of all sizes,
creating great places to live and work, and helping everyone
achieve economic self-sufficiency. OEWD is charged with the
administration of the Local Hiring Policy and is responsible for
Chapter 82 of the San Francisco Administrative Code, the Local
Hiring Policy for Construction, is recognized as one of the strongest
pieces of legislation in the country to promote the utilization of
resident-hiring on locally sponsored projects. The mandatory local
hiring requirement is 30% by trade, and 50% for apprentices.

sections.heading: Page 5
paragraphs: The 2024 Annual Report for the San Francisco Local Hiring Policy for Construction was produced to inform the Board of Supervisors of local hiring participation
achieved between January 1, 2024 and December 31, 2024. The report includes departmental, project, trade and contractor data, and evaluates performance against
workforce requirements as set by Chapter 82 in the San Francisco Administrative Code.
The 183 projects included in this report were awarded and managed by eight departments within the City and County of San Francisco: Mayor’s Office of Housing and
Community Development (MOHCD), Municipal Transportation Agency (MTA), Port of San Francisco (Port), Public Utilities Commission (PUC), Public Works (SFPW),
Recreation and Parks Department (RPD), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and the Department of Real Estate. Also included in this report is data for
privately-funded developments on City-owned property subject to the Local Hiring Policy, including projects awarded by the Department of Real Estate.
OEWD’s goal is to ensure that the Local Hiring Policy for Construction remains beneficial to local workers and the San Francisco economy. In 2024, OEWD closed out
66 projects under this Policy, all of which achieved compliance by reporting sufficient local work hours or creating job opportunities for local residents. By leveraging
the Policy’s requirements, CityBuild’s compliance and employment networking services teams continue to assist local workers with securing employment.
Since the implementation of the Local Hiring Policy, one of the greatest challenges for the construction industry in the last decade has been creating a pipeline of
workers to meet the demands of the work. OEWD continues to address this need through its CityBuild Academy pre-apprentice training program by providing hands-
on training to two cohorts each year, including graduating 89 new apprentices in 2024. Our newest challenge is ensuring that there is sufficient construction work in
San Francisco and the surrounding areas where these graduates advance their careers. As highlighted by this report, total hours worked on projects under the Local
Hiring Policy have decreased by 8% since 2023, with local apprentice participation being reduced by 4%, reflecting a tighter job market for San Francisco workers amid
To maximize opportunities for local residents, OEWD, in collaboration with contractor and union partners, is focusing on the industry's current needs. This includes
prioritizing efforts to coordinate sustainable employment opportunities for both new and experienced workers, while also supporting contractors who face hiring
challenges in the local construction market. OEWD will continue to assess the Policy's impact, and the availability of qualified local workers, using additional data as it
becomes available. OEWD is also deepening partnerships with local community organizations to better address the construction industry's evolving workforce needs.

sections.heading: Page 12
paragraphs: CityBuild Academy aims to meet the demands of the construction industry by providing
comprehensive pre-apprenticeship and construction administration training to San Francisco
residents. The Academy offers a 12-week pre-apprenticeship and construction skills training
program at the City College of San Francisco, Evans Campus. Trainees learn college level math
while learning foundational skills, obtaining industry-recognized certifications, and gaining
knowledge to enter the construction trades as successful new apprentices. Graduates also
obtain an MC3 (Multi-Craft Core Curriculum) Certification, a nationally recognized certificate
offered through the curriculum from the North America's Building Trades Unions. Since 2006,
1,706 San Francisco residents have graduated from CityBuild Academy and special trainings, and
1,461 graduates have secured employment in various construction trades. Through the
Construction Administration and Professional Services Academy (CAPSA) 274 graduates have
attained permanent employment in the construction industry.
